problem: The plotted turn-off waveform is not triangular: it falls from −8 A at 2.2 μs to −2 A at 3.2 μs and then to 0 at 4.0 μs. The negative area of this plot is about 6.6 μC, while the worked example and the formula Qrr = ½ IRRM trr give 8 μC for the same 8 A and 2 μs. A student who measures the area under the figure will not get the example answer.
fix: Make the plotted waveform triangular (from 0 at the zero crossing, straight to −8 A at the peak, straight back to 0 two microseconds later), or keep the soft shape and add a line to the caption: 'the shape is drawn soft; the worked example uses the triangular approximation Qrr = ½ IRRM trr'.

problem: VF is used for two different things: the cut-in voltage (0.8 V to 1.2 V) and the intercept of the linear model vD = VF + iD rd. In a silicon power diode the cut-in is nearer 0.6 V to 0.8 V; 1 V to 1.2 V is the full on-state drop at rated current, which already includes the iD rd part.
fix: Say the cut-in is roughly 0.6 V to 0.8 V for silicon, and give the linear model as vD = V0 + iD rd, where V0 (about 0.7 V to 0.9 V) is the voltage-axis intercept. Keep the exam trap that the on-state drop at high current is larger than V0.

where: Section 1, comparison with an ideal switch
problem: 'A real diode fails all four: it has VF, finite rd, leakage IS, breakdown VBR, and stored charge that delays turn-off' does not map cleanly onto the four ideal properties. rd is part of the on-state behaviour, not a separate failure, and the idea of finite resistance is not one of the four listed properties.
fix: Rewrite as: 'A real diode fails all four. Its on-state drop VF + iD rd is not zero. Its off-state resistance is finite, so a leakage current IS flows. It has a finite breakdown voltage VBR. And it stores charge, so turn-off takes the reverse recovery time trr.'
